message.reasoning:
I need to decide whether to bid or drop out on the current auction.

Tennessee Avenue completes p2's orange monopoly. That group is extremely valuable. I have $545 cash and am considering a bid near $460.

p2 has $844 and could quickly build three houses on the entire orange group for about $900. That would make rent on each space extremely high. I am weighing whether to bid higher or drop out.

A $450 win by p3 would not complete the orange group. I am checking whether p3 could trade Tennessee for Boardwalk with p2, but that swap seems blocked because p3 already owns Park Place.

A trade for Boardwalk would let p3 complete the dark blue group. That would be a nightmare for both p2 and me. I should not let p3 win cheaply. A bid of $451 leaves only $94 cash. I am also checking p1's red properties with houses.

I have enough mortgage backup to survive a low cash position. I am weighing whether to bid $451 and take the lead, or jump higher to discourage p2.

Tennessee's face value is only $180, but completing the orange monopoly makes it worth far more. p2 still has $394 after a $451 bid, so they can continue building. The pink group is split between players.

A $460 bid would still leave me with about $85 cash and mortgage backup. I could bid between $451 and $460. p2 is unlikely to stop at that level. They already bid $411 with $844.

Dropping out now would let p3 and p2 fight over the auction. That bid war would drain whichever player wins. I am weighing whether to avoid spending cash and let the competition settle.

A $550 win for p2 would leave them with only $294 cash, but they could mortgage their other properties to build two houses on each orange space. This confirms that bidding higher against p2 is a good way to drain their build funds. However, winning the auction myself would not complete the orange monopoly, since I do not own the other orange properties.

Tennessee alone is a poor investment at $450 or above. I would pay that much to block p2 from completing the orange monopoly, which is a permanent asset. I am weighing whether spending $451 to $500 on this blocker is too expensive.

I am weighing the auction against other strategic targets. Marvin Gardens would give me two of three yellows, but I still need Atlantic from p3. The Short Line is blocked by p2's B&O, so it cannot complete a fourth railroad. My greens are blocked by p2's Pennsylvania Avenue. States blocks pink, Connecticut blocks p1's light blue, and Mediterranean blocks p3's brown.

Standard Monopoly strategy suggests paying up to $400–500 for an orange blocker. I can later sell it to p2 for a monopoly of my own, or keep it as permanent denial. p3 at $450 is doing the same. The flip risk is why I should own the key myself.

A $451 bid leaves only $94 cash. I am checking rent exposure from States Avenue to see if that is too risky.

I am on States Avenue. p1 auctioned Tennessee after landing there. I will roll next after p2 and p3. I am checking which properties I could reach from here.

A roll of 12 from States Avenue lands on Illinois for $300 rent. A 9 or 11 lands on Indiana or Kentucky for $90. With only $94 cash, I would mortgage to cover the $300 hit. The risk is manageable.

p2 can mortgage their other properties to build three houses on the orange group even after paying $500 or $600 for Tennessee. They have roughly $720 in mortgage value, so they can still afford full construction. The only way to genuinely block them is to bid around $650–$750, where building becomes too slow.

p1 only has $23, so the red properties are not an immediate threat. p2 likely wants to cap their bid around $500–$600 to keep build funds liquid without mortgaging everything. p3 has $803 and may push higher, so I may need to bid $500–$550 to win. I am also weighing whether spending that much on Tennessee would leave me unable to buy Marvin Gardens at face value.

Marvin Gardens is a useful block on p3's yellow group, but it is less urgent than the orange blocker. The yellow set is landed on less frequently and costs only $150 per house to build.

I am now leaning toward bidding $451, the minimum amount needed to stay in control. Jumping to $500 would risk overpaying if p2 and p3 drop out early. p2 will almost certainly bid at least $451.

A $451 bid merely continues the war without winning. I am now considering a higher bid around $500 to signal commitment and force a re-evaluation. Dropping out is rejected because of the flip risk and because owning the key is the best long-term position.

The orange deed is a trade chip worth more than $450. I cannot price p2 out of building because I only have $545. They would still have roughly $343 after paying $501 and could continue building. I must either outbid their maximum or hope they stop before I run out of cash.

p2 has been matching bids incrementally, so they want the property. p3 is more aggressive and may push above $545 to deny p2 or hold the trade chip. I should not drop out before winning at a reasonable price; the worst outcome is p2 acquiring it for a price that still allows them to build.

I am raising my bid cap to about $500–$520. p3’s aggressive bidding confirms the flip risk, so I need a higher ceiling to stay in control and keep the property out of p2’s hands.

A $500 bid leaves only $25–45 cash, but mortgages cover emergencies. The old cap logic says to keep bidding past $460 whenever p2 can still afford to house, since p2 is not too poor to build at that price. This justifies pushing higher than the new $520 ceiling.

The $460 cap was only a liquidity buffer. The real override is that p2 can still afford to build after paying even $600, so I should keep bidding as long as I can afford it and p2 would remain able to house. My absolute maximum is now around $530–$545, leaving only $15–$0 cash, because owning the orange blocker is worth that risk.

I can mortgage my other properties to cover the $300 rent on Illinois even if I have no cash left. I will bid to win or force the price higher.

A $451 bid is the conservative choice. It keeps the auction alive and reveals more about p3's true limit. A jump to $501 might scare p3 into dropping out if they are near a round-number cap, but it also risks overpaying if they are not.

I will bid $501. This leaves $44 cash and forces p2 to match at $502, draining their build funds while signaling commitment.

I am second-guessing the $501 bid. A $460 probe would be safer, since both p2 and p3 might drop out at that price and I could win for $460 instead of overpaying $50. I am weighing whether they will actually stop at $451.

A $451 bid is the safer choice. p2 will match every increment, so a jump to $501 would only overpay by a few dollars if they stop early. Incremental bidding is slightly better for price discovery, and the extra turns are acceptable.

I will bid $451 incrementally to avoid overpaying. Dropping out now would let p2 win the property and complete the orange monopoly, so I must stay in while I can afford it. I will keep the denial framing in my public message.

I will bid $451 and publicly commit to keeping the orange group split. I am raising my cap to about $520, since p2 can still build well above that price and owning the key is worth that risk.

I will bid $500. A $451 increment looks too weak after my earlier jump to $410, and p3 has already raised above me. A larger bid signals commitment and prevents p2 from pushing the price higher.

I will bid $500 and publicly commit to keeping the orange group split. I am not raising to $520 yet; I will reassess next turn based on who is leading. p1 has almost no cash and is not an immediate threat. p3 still needs to finish their yellow, dark blue, and brown sets.

I am now considering an offensive trade: offering p2 Tennessee for Pennsylvania Avenue. That would give p2 the orange monopoly and me the green one. Green is weaker than orange, so the trade may not be worth it unless I can also collect cash or build.

I will not trade Tennessee for Pennsylvania Avenue. Orange is the stronger set, so giving p2 orange would be a losing move. I will keep Tennessee as a permanent block to deny orange to p2. p1 owns the red monopoly but is cash-poor and fragile.

Blocking orange forever leaves p2 with roughly $844 in cash but no monopoly. Dark blue is expensive to build and less landed on, so it poses little threat. I will bid $500 now and keep a small cash buffer.

You are an autonomous player in a game of Monopoly competing against other AI players.

Your goal is to win the game by maximizing long-term advantage and being the last non-bankrupt player. You may use any legal strategy or personality (aggressive, deceptive, cooperative, conservative, manipulative, opportunistic, friendly, hostile, etc.) and may adapt dynamically as the game evolves.

You will receive the following inputs:

1) System Prompt (this message): authoritative instructions.
2) Game State: full board/game context + memory (public chat, recent actions, your private thoughts).
3) Action State: exact dynamic context for the current decision and legal action schemas.

### Action Rules
- Make exactly one tool call per decision.
- Use only tools listed as legal for that decision.
- Never invent tools, arguments, or targets.
- Obey the provided argument schema exactly.
- If a tool requires no arguments, pass none.

### Messages
Each action must include both fields:
- Public Message: visible to other players. Use it to negotiate, bluff, deceive, cooperate, intimidate, joke, or stay silent — whatever best serves your strategy.
- Private Thoughts: visible only to you. Use it to reason honestly, track strategy, analyze opponents, and leave notes for your future self. Be concise but clear.
- Keep both messages token-efficient and concise.

### Strategy Guidance
- Play strategically with long-term outcomes in mind.
- Observe opponents and adapt.
- Deception in public chat is allowed; private thoughts should reflect true reasoning.
- Be consistent unless there is a reason to change.
- Prefer concise reasoning and communication.

Your role is not to explain rules or debug the system.  
Your role is to **play Monopoly and win**.

When a decision is presented, think carefully and make one legal tool call that best advances your chances of winning.

your_private_thoughts_last_10.thought: Reject. States is the 3-way pink block (p2 St. Charles, p3 Virginia). Giving it to p2 creates a 2-pink lever they can use on p3. PA + my NC is only a contingent green; anyone can buy Pacific to deny me, and $200/house means I can't build even if I land on it. List-value gain isn't worth losing a hard block for a race I likely lose. Cash $495 stays for face denial: Tennessee $180, B&O/Short Line $200, Marvin $280, Pacific $300. Keep Connecticut, Ventnor, NC, Mediterranean, States. Do not fuel p2 or p1.

Buy at $300, leave $205. I already own NC; this makes me 2/3 green and leaves p2 with only Pennsylvania, so they cannot complete green without both of my deeds. Auctioning risks handing p2 the second green cheap. No monopoly exists yet, so rent risk is low. $205 still covers Tennessee ($180) face denial. Keep Connecticut, Ventnor, States, Mediterranean, both greens. Do not fuel p1 or p2.

No +EV trade. $205 stays liquid for Tennessee face denial ($180). I am 2/3 green (NC+Pacific); p2's PA is the monopoly key and they will not sell it without a completed set I cannot safely give. Keep all blockers: Connecticut (p1 light blue), States (pink gate vs p2/p3), Ventnor (p3 yellow), Mediterranean (p3 brown). Do not fuel p1 or p2. No mortgage.

Reject. Connecticut is the only hard block on p1's light blue. $260 is worse than the $320 I already refused. They'd keep ~$409 plus mortgage capacity and house immediately at $50/house. Cash doesn't complete a set for me. $205 stays for Tennessee face denial ($180). Keep all blockers: Connecticut, States, Ventnor, Mediterranean, both greens. Do not fuel p1.

No +EV trade. $515 stays liquid for face denial: Tennessee $180 (block p2 orange — they have $831 and 2/3), Marvin $280 (2/3 yellow with Ventnor; block p3), then B&O/Short Line (I own both RRs). Do not sell Connecticut (p1 light blue), States (pink gate vs p2/p3), Ventnor, Mediterranean (p3 brown), or either green. Do not give p1 cash — reds already have 1 house and they're at $19; cash lets them build. Greens need PA from p2 and $200/house; can't safely fund. No mortgage.

No +EV trade. $545 stays liquid for face denial: Tennessee $180 (block p2 orange — St James+NY, they have $794), Marvin $280 (2/3 yellow with Ventnor; block p3), Short Line $200 (would make 3 RRs). Do not sell Connecticut (p1 light blue; they already have built reds and only $67), States (pink gate vs p2 St Charles / p3 Virginia), Ventnor, Mediterranean (p3 brown), or either green. PA from p2 would complete green but $200/house and even-build means I can't house it without draining the Tennessee reserve; p2 won't sell the blocker cheap. Don't give p1 cash. No mortgage.

Lowball. States is the pink gate (p2 has St. Charles). Giving it up only if I also get Virginia AND Atlantic: then I’m 2/3 yellow (Ventnor+Atlantic) and can still deny Marvin, and p3 is only 2/3 pink with me holding nothing… wait I would NOT hold States, so p3 has Virginia only plus I gave States so p3 has States+Virginia = 2/3 pink, p2 has St Charles. That’s handing p3 a 2-pink lever. Atlantic+Ventnor is 2/3 yellow which is good only if I later get Marvin. $250 cuts Tennessee reserve ($545-250=$295, still covers Marvin $280 or Tennessee $180 but not both). They will reject. Do not sweeten. If they somehow accept, I must not sell Ventnor and must prioritize Marvin. Float only.

p3 rejected States+$250 for Virginia+Atlantic; do not sweeten. No +EV trade. $545 stays liquid for face denial: Tennessee $180 first (block p2 orange — St James+NY, $844 to build), then Marvin $280 (2/3 yellow with Ventnor; block p3), then Short Line $200. Do not sell Connecticut (p1 light blue), States (pink gate), Ventnor, Mediterranean, or either green. PA completes green but $200/house and even-build; p2 will not sell the key cheap. Do not give p1 cash — reds already built, they are at $23. No mortgage.

Stay in. Tennessee completes p2 orange (St James+NY, $844 to build). Winning at $260 is fine denial; cash left $285. Prefer p3 or me over p2. Cap ~$400 so p2 cannot buy it and still house hard; above that drop and let p3 pay if they will. Do not drop while p2 can still take it cheap. Marvin/Short Line secondary to this block.

Own the orange key if I can. If p3 wins, they can flip Tennessee to p2 for Boardwalk and both get monopolies. Cap ~$460 (leaves ~$85; mortgage backup for p1 Illinois 2h=$300). Above that, drop only if p2 is too poor to house. Prefer me over p3 over p2. Marvin/Short Line secondary.
